extracted.intended_audience: readers/travelers/diplomats interested in Japanese court etiquette, imperial ceremonies, and education
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive rules about Imperial Court regulations, orders/precedence, invitation rights, ceremonial sequences (New Year’s Audience, Court Ball), and related social-educational practices in early-20th-century Japan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperial Court regulated by law (peerage and nominal honours 'ikai'/'kurai')
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything important connected with the Imperial Court of Japan is regulated by law. These regulations include, not only the Peerage of all ranks, but also those natives who belong to the civil service or who have been judged deserving of recognition on account of some special contribution to the public welfare. The latter system of nominal honours is called 'ikai,' or more commonly 'kurai'; but it has no outward badge to represent it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holders of a fourth or higher grade of 'ikai,' even when no longer in Government service, receive an invitation on the occasion of certain state festivals (e.g., the Birthday evening party). The heir of a Peer is entitled to the fifth-grade junior 'ikai' as soon as he reaches his majority. Wealthy merchants may possess this nominal honour by contributions of money to public purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decorations determine court rank (orders and class correspondence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decorations have prescribed court rank according to the Order and the Degree of the decoration conferred. Foreigners having decorations come in the same position as natives of the same Order and Class of decoration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: those who have the 2nd Class Order of the Rising Sun have with it a court rank between the Counts and the Viscounts; those who have the 3d Class fall between the Viscounts and the Barons. The actual arrangement of precedence is fixed (e.g., listed in the 'Japanese Year Book') and should not be meddled with by the inexpert foreigner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of the Rising Sun: grades and significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the decorations, the six grades of 'The Order of the Rising Sun' are the most coveted; because this Order is bestowed only for 'conspicuous personal merit'; and hitherto it has been only sparingly bestowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the Grand Order of Merit and The Grand Cordon of the Chrysanthemum are added to the First Class of the Rising Sun, the fortunate person has been invested with the highest honour accessible to a Japanese subject. Only a very small number of personages attain so high an honour (examples: Prince Ito, Yamagata, Oyama, Matsukata, Admiral Togo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invitation rights tied to holders of Orders (who may request invitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Holders of the 3d and higher classes of the 'Orders of Merit' have the right to request cards of invitation to certain of the Court functions, attendance at which is a much coveted privilege.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreigners may obtain invitations either through the official representative (ambassador) of their country or through an influential native friend; but for certain functions this is very difficult or impossible. Accredited representatives of foreign countries are entitled to special treatment; otherwise, no one not actually invited can lay claim to a 'right' of attendance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Etiquette about attendance and invitations (do not go where not desired)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an essential effect of the sentiment that exalts personal worthiness above court rank not to wish to go where one is not desired, or where one’s presence is not in every way an appropriate part of the social or ceremonial occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issuing invitations to everybody would deprive the particular function of meaning and be a physical impossibility. From the guest's side, a self-respecting person should not desire to attend where not wanted; complaints by foreigners about exclusion are common but misplaced in view of these social realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of the Court Ball (what to expect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court Ball (e.g., given by the Minister of Foreign Affairs on the Emperor’s birthday) is more a formal assembly than a dancing party: many nobles and officials attend, but few dance; Japanese ladies generally do not enjoy dancing in native costume, and many men of mark regard dancing as unmanly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accommodations may be greatly enlarged by temporary structures; decorations mix lavishness and reserve with national symbols. The event affords opportunity for meeting eminent persons and receiving or offering salutations, but should not be expected to resemble Western-style balls or garden entertainments.

rubrics_metrics.name: New Year’s Audience sequence and who attends (ceremonial order)
rubrics_metrics.description: New Year’s Audiences are the most stately and formal functions: on Jan 1 the Imperial Princes go earliest; then the highest ranks of nobility; and in due succession, according to court rank, come diplomats, higher officials in army/navy/state, holders of decorations of Third and higher Classes, certain professors, and Shintō priests; four groups take their turns during successive morning hours. Foreign diplomats are received in early afternoon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sequence is strictly regulated and ceremonial; the capital is decked in characteristic fashion and the occasion carries symbolic decorations (pine, bamboo, fern leaves, Shintō prayer papers, food symbols) signifying peace, plenty, and long life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program template for a ceremonial school event
rubrics_metrics.description: A typical morning programme for visiting dignitaries at a country school, as itemised: (1) Visiting the recitation rooms; (2) Salutation (all together); (3) introduction (the Principal); (4) singing a welcome song (the pupils); (5) address of welcome (a pupil); (6) sketch of the school (a pupil); (7) welcome (Mr. K. Hamaguchi); (8) Address (Professor Ladd); (9) Thanks (the Principal); (10) singing of a school song; (11) (dismission).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The morning is devoted to pupils and patrons; the afternoon to teachers. Under some circumstances ignorance of the language spares the foreign speaker certain embarrassments when being praised or blamed. Programs are deliberately elaborate to impress visitors and to show the community’s value placed on education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideals of the Teacher and public education priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: The Imperial Rescript ideal is steadily held up: that there shall be no household in the land, and no member of any household, to whom the benefits of education shall not have been supplied in liberal measure. Despite this ideal, Normal Schools, Higher Schools, and Universities can scarcely provide for more than one-tenth of those desirous of advanced training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-school teachers are heavily overworked and lamentably underpaid; nevertheless they display eagerness to avail themselves of opportunities to improve. Examples (e.g., voluntary class of over 800 teachers for 20 hours of lectures) illustrate teacher dedication as a valued criterion of educational quality and outreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community veneration and the social value of public service (the 'spirit of Hamaguchi')
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'spirit of Hamaguchi Gōryo'—a local reverence for lives of service—manifests as a felt spiritual presence of great rulers, teachers, and heroes; this veneration (described by Hearn as 'ghosts' or 'living gods') binds living and dead, fosters unity, and inspires self-sacrifice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This attitude is credited with strengthening spiritual training (e.g., of soldiers) and making sacrifice more prompt and cheerful. It is regarded as an admirable and hopeful social force that promotes civic virtue and national cohesion.
